title: Pilot study: Quantitative and qualitative movement analysis for early detection of joint damage in patients with haemophilia
summary: Severe congenital bleeding tendencies (haemophilia, "haemophiliacs") with joint bleeding are associated with changes in movement patterns. A person with joint disease moves differently or has pain during movements. As a result, he is inhibited in his range of motion and in his normal development. We can detect many changes in movement patterns through observation, but smaller changes are often not noticed and can still lead to impairment. The aim of this study is to detect these small changes in movement at an early stage in order to prevent further damage if possible. For this purpose, the new method of gait analysis will be applied by means of videos and evaluation via a computer programme and it will be investigated whether this new method can correctly detect joint damage. In addition, normal daily activity will be determined over the course of a week and physical activity and health-related quality of life will be assessed with the help of questionnaires. These examinations will be repeated at 12-month intervals and the results will be compared with those of healthy volunteers. The overall aim of the study is to improve the joint health of haemophilia patients and to detect damage in the joints at an early stage.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. informed consent of the test person himself/herself or, in the case of minors, also of a guardian.
2. have a confirmed severe or moderate haemophilia or
3. healthy subjects, who are both age and sex-matched to an already included patient and do not suffer from any joint diseases, neurological or musculoskeletal complaints.
Exclusion criteria:
Explicit reservation by patients or subjects or their carers against participation in the study, or lack of written consent by the volunteers/patients and, in the case of minors, also by the parents (in the case of infants up to 6 years of age, only by the parents). Further exclusion criteria are the completion of the 30th year of age, existing language barriers that preclude consent or the inability to walk an 8 m distance without an aid.
Healthy volunteers are excluded if they have had a serious injury within the last 6 months.
